parts.layout_phase: Beginning of the Intermediate III phase, between Strata 6 and 7 (Marshall); 'Intermediate Period' (Wheeler 1950 excavation)
parts.what_was_built: Marshall reports that 'at the beginning of Intermediate III Period, i.e. between strata 6 and 7, an immense artificial terrace of unburnt brick and clay was raised' under the later Buddhist stupa and monastery, lifting the buildings of the 6th and later strata about 22 feet above their neighbours (vol. I p. 10). In the Stupa Area the 20-foot interval between the 6th and 7th strata is 'occupied almost entirely by crude brick or alluvial mud heaped up artificially so as to form an immense platform over the whole of this Stupa area, as well as over a big expanse of ground to the north of it', held by retaining walls found on the east (RR, Banerji 1921-22) and west (TT, Mackay 1927-28) (vol. I p. 125, side-note 'Construction of lofty platform in Intermediate III Period'). Wheeler, after his 1950 deep cutting west of the Granary, wrote that the 'artificial platform of the citadel is built of mud-brick and mud' and that 'its construction dates from the optimum phase of the city's development as we know it, the so-called Intermediate Period', to which the Great Bath and Granary also belong, but that 'under it lie other buildings and phases to an unexplored depth' (1968 pp. 37-38).
parts.locator: marshall1931mohenjodaro vol. I pp. 10, 125; wheeler1968indus pp. 37-38
parts.excavator_basis: Cross-dating, no radiocarbon. Marshall (vol. I ch. VIII, pp. 102-107) assigned the Indus seals found at Ur and Kish provisionally to the Intermediate Period and concluded that 'the occupation of Mohenjo-daro fell approximately between 3250 and 2750 B.C.' (p. 104), with the antiquities 'not earlier than 3250 B.C.' (p. 106). This bracket covers the whole excavated occupation, not the platform alone. Mackay's pottery chapter in the same volume (p. 334) dates the Early Period c. 3250 B.C. and the Intermediate Period c. 3000 B.C. by Susa II and Jemdet Nasr parallels, which puts the start of the platform, at the Early-Intermediate boundary, near 3000 B.C. on that reckoning.

syntheses.statement: Wheeler, as excavator of the 1950 cutting, set the city's founding by Mesopotamian contacts and the first radiocarbon dates: 'the nuclear cities of the Indus civilization were founded sometime before 2400 B.C. and ... endured in some shape to the eighteenth century B.C.' (p. 125). Dales's 1964-65 borings showing occupation 39 feet below the plain led him to add that 'the Indus civilization was a going concern well before 2400 B.C.' (p. 120).
syntheses.disagreement: Places the founding of the city, and so of its platform, some five to eight centuries later than Marshall's 3250-2750 B.C. bracket.

syntheses.statement: Jansen reads the citadel as a single founding platform: a mud-brick retaining construction with an inner filling of alluvial sediment, about 400,000 cubic metres, whose internal layers 'could have been found by the excavators ... not as strata of different phases over a long timespan but as strata of a very short construction period' (p. 13). He concludes that 'the first urban settlement of Mohenjo-Daro was constructed as a whole in a very short period of only a few years' within 'a rather small time gap of not more than 80 years around 2400 B.C.' (p. 15), and that the platforms mark the beginning of the mature Harappan period at the site.
syntheses.disagreement: Rejects the Marshall-Mackay stratification on which the 'Intermediate III' attribution rests and makes the platform the founding act of the city around 2400 B.C., not a construction inserted after an Early Period.

syntheses.page: Kenoyer 1998, Ancient Cities of the Indus Valley Civilization, p. 25, as quoted on the page
syntheses.statement: Kenoyer writes that 'the formation of large urban centers such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, located in the core areas of the Indus Valley, can be dated from around 2600 to 1900 B.C.', and that Dales's 1964-65 radiocarbon samples came only from the latest levels because the earliest lie below the water table.
syntheses.disagreement: A general urban-phase bracket, later than Marshall's and earlier than Wheeler's and Jansen's start; it does not date the platform itself.

parts.conflicts: Three readings of when the platform was built stand side by side. Marshall places it at the start of Intermediate III, after at least one Early Period stratum, and dates the occupation 3250-2750 B.C. by Mesopotamian cross-dating. Wheeler agrees that it belongs to the Intermediate Period with earlier buildings beneath, but dates the city's foundation to before 2400 B.C. Jansen treats it as the founding platform of the whole city, built in a few years around 2400 B.C., and doubts the long multi-phase growth implied by the strata. No radiocarbon date comes from the platform. The 2025-26 excavations dated the perimeter wall at the platform's western edge (next part), not the platform fill.

parts.part: citadel perimeter: mud-brick 'bund' or city wall at the western foot of the citadel (Wheeler's 1950 cutting west of the Granary, reopened in 2025-26 as trench MD25)
parts.layout_phase: First city wall, end of the Early Harappan or Kot Diji phase (Kenoyer, Ibrahim and Lashari 2026); built 'at a relatively early date' in the citadel's history (Wheeler)
parts.what_was_built: Wheeler found that 'the citadel-platform had to be protected wholly or in part by a mud-brick embankment or bund 43 feet wide at a relatively early date', that a large burnt-brick drain along the foot of the platform was at the same time rebuilt 14 feet higher, and that 'later the bund was itself reinforced externally' (1968 p. 38); his section facing p. 44 shows the bund resting on 'floors' that continue below the March 1950 water level, with a later mud-brick addition on its outer face. The 2025-26 Pakistani-American excavations re-exposed this structure, which Kenoyer describes as 'the ancient city wall or mud brick platform', its western edge at about 47.74 m above sea level, a combined width of about 6.5 m with eroded edges, bricks about 10 x 20 x 40 cm, and a repair or addition along the western edge (Preliminary Report p. 4, quoted in the Friday Times). Dawn reports the team's view that the wall 'was built in many phases and the earliest structure was built on top of an even earlier occupation deposit'.
parts.locator: wheeler1968indus p. 38 and section facing p. 44; fridaytimes2026defences (quoting Kenoyer, Ibrahim and Lashari 2026, Preliminary Report of the Mohenjo-Daro Excavations 2025-26, pp. 4, 6-8); dawn2026mohenjodaro
parts.excavator_basis: Radiocarbon and pottery. Charcoal from Core 5 (lot MD25-262) in the lower levels of the wall gave 2708-2576 cal BC at 50% probability; Kenoyer reads it as 'the first concrete radiocarbon date for the Early Harappan wall at Mohenjo-daro' and compares it with the Early Harappan wall at Harappa, 2800-2600 BC (Preliminary Report p. 8, via the Friday Times). Dawn reports the conclusion as 'constructed at the end of the Early Harappan or Kot Diji Phase, around 2700-2600 BCE, approximately 100 years before the beginning of the Harappan Phase', with later wall phases from about 2600 BCE maintained until about 2200 BCE. Wheeler gave no absolute date for the bund.

radiocarbon.context: Core 5, depth 1.8-2.0 m, cored in the lower levels of the mud-brick perimeter wall; level associated with street levels containing Context A or Early Harappan pottery; one non-diagnostic sherd in the sample
radiocarbon.phase: Early Harappan wall construction (first city wall)
radiocarbon.note: Quoted from Kenoyer, Ibrahim and Lashari, Preliminary Report of the Mohenjo-Daro Excavations 2025-26 (31 pp., submitted to the Directorate General of Antiquities and Archaeology, Government of Sindh, 16 March 2026; unpublished). Neither the conventional age, the laboratory number nor the calibration curve is quoted; the Friday Times gives 20 February 2026 as the date the results were received, and Dawn reports that the dating was done in the United States.

radiocarbon.lab_no: not published (field lots MD25-251 and MD25-252)
radiocarbon.context: Operation 2, interior of the city wall: upper levels of street deposits (dumps of pottery, bone, ash and charcoal) sealed by layers of eroded mud brick from the perimeter wall
radiocarbon.phase: post-construction street deposits, equated by Kenoyer with Harappa Period 3B; wall no longer maintained
radiocarbon.calibrated_published: around 2460 to 2280 cal BC (87 to 94% confidence level)
radiocarbon.note: A terminus ante quem for the wall: Kenoyer infers that 'the perimeter or city wall was not being maintained and was beginning to erode' by this time. The quotation gives one range for both lots; how many determinations it summarises is not stated.

radiocarbon.lab_no: not published (field lots MD25-253 and MD25-254, first result)
radiocarbon.context: Operation 2, lower levels of the upper street layers on the interior of the city wall
radiocarbon.note: Quoted from the unpublished 2026 Preliminary Report.

radiocarbon.lab_no: not published (field lots MD25-253 and MD25-254, second result)
radiocarbon.context: Operation 2, lower levels of the upper street layers on the interior of the city wall
radiocarbon.note: Kenoyer attributes this result to 'someone burning old wood and dumping this along with more recent burned wood', so the excavators do not use it to date the street layer.

syntheses.page: quoting Alcock 1952, Quarterly Pakistan (Karachi, January 1952), pp. 12-16
syntheses.statement: Leslie Alcock, Wheeler's assistant in 1950, wrote that the massive mud-brick wall found below the plain 'goes back to a considerably earlier period than that of the Granary and the other buildings of the Citadel, and indeed it was probably in ruins when the Citadel was raised. But there are no convincing signs of a defensive wall in the Citadel period.'
syntheses.disagreement: Makes the wall older than, and unrelated in use to, the citadel platform, whereas Wheeler has it protecting the platform and the 2026 excavators have it maintained into the Harappa phase until about 2200 BCE.

syntheses.statement: Re-reading Wheeler's unpublished and published sections, Jansen concludes that the 'mud-brick bund seems to have been erected in at least three stages', the lowest at 45 m above sea level and below, that a drain and 'floors' to its west may be a street built against the oldest bund, that structures continue down to at least 41 m above sea level, and that the bund may be the retaining wall of 'a gigantic platform' with alluvial infill on which the Granary stands.
syntheses.disagreement: Treats the bund as the retaining wall of the founding platform, built in a short construction episode, rather than a flood bund added later or an older defensive wall.

syntheses.statement: Reports, from a member of the Technical Consultative Committee of the National Fund for Mohenjo Daro and from Dr Asma Ibrahim, five new radiocarbon dates for the perimeter wall; the first wall at the end of the Early Harappan or Kot Diji phase around 2700-2600 BCE; later wall phases in the Harappa phase from about 2600 BCE, 'expanded and maintained until around 2200 BCE and possibly even longer'; Wheeler 'misidentified it as a revetment or flood protective bund'.

Summarises the new dates as showing that the city 'was occupied as early as 2700 to 2600 B.C., about two hundred years earlier than previously thought', with samples from the mud-brick wall surrounding the western Stupa Mound.
syntheses.disagreement: Presents the wall date as the start of occupation, whereas the excavators place a Kot Dijian occupation below and before the first wall.

parts.conflicts: The structure has been read four ways: Wheeler's flood bund added to an existing platform 'at a relatively early date'; Alcock's much older wall already in ruins when the citadel was raised; Jansen's retaining wall of the founding platform built in three stages; and the 2026 team's multi-phase city wall first built about 2700-2600 BCE and kept up to about 2200 BCE. The 2026 evidence itself has loose ends. Kenoyer's report also states that Kot Dijian sherds in the mortar show 'the lowest section of the mud brick city wall dates to the Kot Dijian Period, approximately 3300-2800 BC' (p. 6), which conflicts with the 2700-2600 BCE radiocarbon placement unless the sherds are read as residual. The key date carries only a 50% probability range, no conventional age or laboratory number has been released, Dawn counts five dates where the Friday Times quotation gives four results, and the report remains unpublished.

parts.part: lower town (DK-G, HR and VS areas): street grid
parts.layout_phase: Intermediate III phase, the lowest level at which the street grid has been exposed (Mackay 1938, who reassigns Intermediate III to the end of the Early Period)
parts.what_was_built: Mackay writes that 'the plans in Pls. XVI to XX show how carefully the G Section of the DK Area was laid out' and that First Street, traceable from DK-G to the southern limit of the HR Area, 'has been excavated down to the foundation level of the Intermediate III occupation', where it was 30 ft 3 in to 32 ft wide (average level -20.4 ft below datum), with Crooked Lane and other lanes opening into it and a drain first built in Intermediate III (pp. 25-27). He adds that the street was raised with each rebuilding 'while the alignment of the street remained the same well into the Intermediate I Phase' (p. 27). Below this level the grid is not known: in DK-G Block 7 a thick mud-brick platform with its base at -28 ft overlay rubble down to -35 ft and a small two-roomed building with a pavement at -35 ft, and sub-soil water stopped work at -38.5 ft on 7 March 1931 (pp. 42-43). Marshall describes the same process of raising lanes, side streets and drains to 'higher and higher levels' (vol. I p. 9).
parts.locator: mackay1938further pp. xiv-xv, 25-27, 42-43; marshall1931mohenjodaro vol. I p. 9
parts.excavator_basis: Cross-dating, no radiocarbon. Mackay dates the upper levels to about 2500 B.C. by Indus objects in Akkadian buildings at Tell Asmar (amending Marshall's 2750 B.C.), and the lowest attainable levels to about 2800 B.C. by a chlorite-schist vessel fragment found 28.1 ft below datum, from beneath the DK-G mud-brick platform, matching a Susa II jar, which 'allows some three hundred years between the uppermost and the lowest attainable levels' (p. 7). The bracket covers the whole exposed sequence; the Intermediate III street level lies within it, above the 2800 B.C. horizon.

syntheses.statement: Dales reports that test drilling in the 1964-65 season showed that 'occupation at our particular area of the city begins thirty-nine feet below plain level', with ground water only fifteen feet below the plain, so that the earliest levels lie more than 25 feet below the water table.

From Dales's two borings near the HR mound Wheeler infers 'something like 13 feet of waterlogged accumulation' below the lowest level reached by open excavation, and 'a very appreciable accumulation of occupation-debris at Mohenjo-daro beneath the levels which yielded Indus materials of the kind recognized in Akkadian and perhaps pre-Akkadian strata at Tell Asmar'.
syntheses.disagreement: Implies a long occupation below the exposed grid without dating its start; Wheeler doubts how far the boring material can be identified as Indus.

syntheses.statement: Jansen notes that the lowest proven construction level in the lower city is a drain 30 feet below datum (45.47 m above sea level) in DK-G, that the Marshall-Mackay stratification 'based on regular horizontal growth has been outdated now for a long time', that the lower town too may stand on a platform (the two platforms together about 4 million cubic metres), and that the whole first urban settlement was built within a few years around 2400 B.C.
syntheses.disagreement: Rejects Mackay's phase scheme and his 2800 B.C. date for the lowest levels; puts the founding of the planned city around 2400 B.C.

syntheses.statement: Mandal's review of Indian radiocarbon dates finds that all seven Mohenjo-daro dates then available (TF-75 and the six Pennsylvania dates) belong to the Late Phase and that 'we have no radiocarbon date for the Early Phase of the Central Harappa'.

syntheses.page: online essay by J. M. Kenoyer
syntheses.statement: Kenoyer writes that the structures visible today mostly belong to the final Harappa-phase and Late Harappan occupation, that the radiocarbon dates from the mixed later levels place the final occupation of the HR area between 2200 and 1900 BCE, and that the earliest occupation levels lie below the water table and 'date to around 3500 BCE, during the Kot Diji phase'.
syntheses.disagreement: Puts an Early Harappan occupation under the city, against Jansen's view that there is 'hardly any proof for an earlier settlement below mature Harappan layers'.

syntheses.page: Kenoyer 1998, Ancient Cities of the Indus Valley Civilization, p. 25, as quoted on the page
syntheses.statement: The formation of large urban centres such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa 'can be dated from around 2600 to 1900 B.C.'; the origins of Mohenjo-daro 'remain obscure' because the earliest levels are submerged.
syntheses.disagreement: Later than Mackay's c. 2800 B.C. for the lowest attainable levels and earlier than Jansen's c. 2400 B.C. founding.

parts.conflicts: No radiocarbon date comes from the layout phase or the phase before it; all published determinations from the lower town are from the latest levels (see notes). The start of the grid is dated only by cross-dating (Mackay, c. 2800-2500 B.C. for the exposed sequence), by general syntheses (Kenoyer, from about 2600 B.C.) and by Jansen's model of a city founded in a few years around 2400 B.C. The phase labels themselves shifted: Mackay moved Intermediate III into the Early Period and Late III into the Intermediate Period, while Jansen rejects the scheme. Marshall's datum (the earliest Buddhist pavement on the Stupa mound) and Mackay's DK-G bench level (178.7 ft above mean sea level) differ, so depths below datum cannot be compared directly between the two reports.

first_occupation.phase: Kot Diji (Early Harappan) phase, below the present water table; known only from cores and from sherds in the mortar of the earliest perimeter wall
first_occupation.basis: Cross-dating of pottery, no radiocarbon. Kenoyer, Ibrahim and Lashari's 2026 Preliminary Report (p. 6, quoted in the Friday Times) states that Kot Dijian pottery from deep coring below the first mud-brick perimeter wall 'provides clear indication of the presence of Kot Dijian occupation prior to the construction of the first mud brick perimeter wall', and dates the Kot Dijian Period 'approximately 3300-2800 BC based on comparative pottery at Harappa and other Sites'; Kenoyer added on 25 March 2026 that 'the date for the lowest levels has not been collected yet'. Kenoyer's harappa.com essay puts the earliest levels 'around 3500 BCE'. The older excavations never reached natural soil: Mackay stopped at -38.5 ft below datum in DK-G (1938 pp. xiv, 43), Wheeler's 1950 cutting stopped 26 feet below the plain at the surface of an occupation layer under the Granary's foundations (1968 p. 119), and Dales's borings found occupation beginning 39 feet below plain level in the HR area (Expedition 1965). Jansen (1987 p. 15) saw 'hardly any proof for an earlier settlement below mature Harappan layers'.

notes: Mohenjo-daro has two parts with different histories. The western mound (citadel) stands on a mud-brick platform that Marshall and Wheeler assign to the Intermediate Period, edged on the west by a massive mud-brick wall or bund that Wheeler cut in 1950 and a Pakistani-American team led by J. M. Kenoyer, Asma Ibrahim and Ali Lashari re-excavated in 2025-26. The lower town's street grid has been exposed down to Mackay's Intermediate III level in DK-G; nothing is known of its plan below that, and the earliest occupation lies under the water table, reached only by borings and cores. The only dated evidence that bears on when any part of the layout was built is the 2026 result for the first perimeter wall, 2708-2576 cal BC at 50% probability, which we know only from the Friday Times' quotation of the unpublished Preliminary Report; we record it with the field lot number in place of a laboratory number and with the conventional age left empty because neither has been released. All other published radiocarbon dates from Mohenjo-daro come from late levels and do not date the layout, so we keep them out of the radiocarbon lists: P-1176 3801 +/- 59, P-1177 3985 +/- 64, P-1178A 3802 +/- 59, P-1179 3913 +/- 64, P-1180 3828 +/- 61 and P-1182A 3702 +/- 63 BP (5568 half-life; 'latest level of mature Harappan period along top of W edge of HR mound', Dales 1964-65; rc-penn-x pp. 333-334), and TF-75 3600 +/- 110 BP (5568 half-life; charred grain from 'the pavement of a late date', Chamber 60, Block 2, 1.27 m below datum, Marshall's field no. L855; rc-tf-ii p. 231). Wheeler (1968 pp. 122-124) reprints these on both half-lives, for example TF-75 as 1760 B.C. +/- 115 (5730) and 1650 B.C. +/- 110 (5568). We found no published Bayesian model for the site. Kenoyer's harappa.com essay says Wheeler found the early levels at the citadel's north-west corner in 1946, whereas Wheeler's own account dates his Mohenjo-daro cutting to 1950; we take 1950 from Wheeler. The press items arkeonews.net and ancientist.com (saved under data/raw/2026-10-21-town-axes/dating/mohenjo-daro/) only restate Dawn and are not cited. Sources we sought and could not open: Dales and Kenoyer 1986, Excavations at Mohenjo Daro, Pakistan: The Pottery (archive.org item excavationsatmoh0000dale is lending-restricted); Possehl 2002, The Indus Civilization (induscivilizatio0000poss, lending-restricted), and Possehl's 1989 and 1999 compilations (not found online); Dales 1965 in Archaeology 18; Alcock 1952 (known only through the Friday Times quotation); the 2026 Preliminary Report itself; and Jansen 1993 on the wells and drains. The file research/literature/sources/kenoyer_1998_ancient_cities.pdf held locally is not Kenoyer's book but an unrelated decipherment paper, so Kenoyer 1998 is cited through harappa.com. Marshall 1931, Mackay 1938 and Jansen and Urban 1987 are image-only scans; we read them through Tesseract OCR of every page and checked the quoted figures on Marshall p. 334 and Jansen p. 15 against the page images.
